Background Recovery from coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) can be impaired by the persistence of symptoms or new-onset health complications, commonly referred to as Long COVID. In a subset of patients, Long COVID is associated with immune system perturbations of unknown etiology, which could be related to compromised immunoregulatory mechanisms. Objective The objective of this scoping review was to summarize the existing literature regarding the frequency and functionality of Tregs in convalescent COVID-19 patients and to explore indications for their potential involvement in the development of Long COVID Design A systematic search of studies investigating Tregs during COVID-19 convalescence was conducted on MEDLINE ( via Pubmed) and Web of Science. Results The literature search yielded 17 relevant studies, of which three included a distinct cohort of patients with Long COVID. The reviewed studies suggest that the Treg population of COVID-19 patients can reconstitute quantitatively and functionally during recovery. However, the comparison between recovered and seronegative controls revealed that an infection-induced dysregulation of the Treg compartment can be sustained for at least several months. The small number of studies investigating Tregs in Long COVID allowed no firm conclusions to be drawn about their involvement in the syndrome’s etiology. Yet, even almost one year post-infection Long COVID patients exhibit significantly altered proportions of Tregs within the CD4+ T cell population. Conclusions Persistent alterations in cell frequency in Long COVID patients indicate that Treg dysregulation might be linked to immune system-associated sequelae. Future studies should aim to address the association of Treg adaptations with different symptom clusters and blood parameters beyond the sole quantification of cell frequencies while adhering to consensualized phenotyping strategies. regulatory T cells (T reg) COVID-19 SARS-CoV-2 Long Covid immune system adaptive immunity 1 Introduction Infections with the severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2), the pathogen responsible for the ongoing coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) pandemic, manifest with varying severity. The clinical spectrum ranges from asymptomatic/mild disease to severe pneumonia and respiratory distress syndrome that can ultimately lead to death ( 1 , 2 ). Although the majority of patients experience moderate symptoms such as fever, cough, dyspnea, loss of smell and taste or sore throat, it has been highlighted that COVID-19 can include multi-system complications, such as thrombotic events, vasculitis and myocarditis ( 3 – 5 ). In addition to that, the clinical spectrum of COVID-19 encompasses acute immunopathology. Specifically, dysfunctional cellular and humoral immune responses characterized by exaggerated cytokine release, lymphopenia and new onset or aggravated autoimmunity are associated with negative disease outcomes ( 1 , 6 – 9 ). It is estimated that approximately one in eight patients who contracted COVID-19 experience symptoms beyond the acute symptomatic phase, as reported by a recent observational cohort study ( 10 ). The World Health Organization (WHO) defines these sequelae, by common usage now also referred to as “Long COVID”, as a post-COVID-19 condition that usually occurs three months after a confirmed or probable SARS-CoV-2 infection with a set of new-onset, persistent or fluctuating symptoms that last for at least two months ( 11 ). The most common symptoms in this context are fatigue, exercise intolerance, post-exertional malaise, difficulty breathing, headache, muscle pain, tachycardia, concentration deficits and diminished quality of life ( 12 – 15 ). In this context, it bears noting that the overall prevalence and types of symptoms can vary depending on the COVID-19 disease severity. Specifically, the proportion of patients that experience residual symptoms appears to be higher among previously hospitalized patients ( 16 – 18 ). In addition, the results of a clustering analysis conducted as a part of the REACT-2 study suggest that patients with severe initial symptoms report post-acute respiratory symptoms more often than those with mild or asymptomatic COVID-19 whose symptomatology is rather fatigue-dominant ( 19 ). Likewise, recent evidence suggests that those who had one or multiple reinfections exhibit an increased risk of experiencing post-acute sequelae compared to those who were infected once ( 20 ). The pathophysiological mechanisms involved in the devolvement of Long COVID remain to be elucidated, with a range of theories currently under discussion. Merad et al. ( 21 ), for instance, postulated that immunopathological processes, such as chronic inflammation with viral persistence, post-viral autoimmunity, microbiome dysbiosis and unrepaired tissue damage might contribute to the pathophysiology of the Long COVID phenotype. In line with that, it has been documented that affected patients exhibit a significant elevation of multiple inflammatory markers compared to recovered subjects, indicating a dysregulated and overactive immune system ( 22 , 23 ). Correspondingly, the triad of pro-inflammatory cytokines IL-1β, IL-6 and TNF-α showed a significant correlation with persistent symptoms of COVID-19 at an eight-months follow-up ( 24 ). In addition, the discovery of functional autoantibodies specific to G-protein coupled receptors ( 25 ) has been linked to an autonomic dysregulation and assumed to be a cause of residual symptoms ( 26 ). Despite this, components of the immune system that regulate and fine-tune (auto)immune responses, favoring immune homeostasis, such as regulatory T cells (Tregs), have only been investigated sparsely in COVID-19 convalescence and Long COVID. Tregs are a dynamic CD4 + T cell subpopulation that is characterized by CD25 (IL-2 receptor α-chain) upregulation, CD127 (IL-7 receptor α-chain) downregulation and expression of the transcription factor forkhead box P3 (FoxP3) that is considered the master regulator of Treg development ( 27 – 30 ). It is estimated that 80% of the peripheral cell repertoire is represented by functionally mature natural Tregs that develop in the thymus as antigen-primed cells ( 31 , 32 ), while peripherally-derived Tregs are induced from naïve T cells upon antigen encounter ( 32 – 34 ) ( Figure 1 ). During self-directed and pathogen-directed immune responses, activated Tregs exert suppressive effects on effector cells and antigen-presenting cells, for example, through the secretion of the inhibitory cytokines IL-10, IL-35 and TGF-β, by limiting the amount of IL-2 available for conventional T cells or by stimulating the formation of indoleamine 2, 3-dioxygenase ( 28 , 35 ) ( Figure 1 ). In this way, Tregs promote self-tolerance and prevent excessive inflammation, which makes their proper functioning indispensable for a balanced immune response. Correspondingly, diseases such as type 1 diabetes, multiple sclerosis, lupus erythematosus and rheumatoid arthritis are associated with functional deficiencies in the Treg compartment and altered cell frequencies ( 36 , 37 ). Studying COVID-19, previous reviews have already made an effort to characterize Tregs during the acute phase of a SARS-CoV-2-infection ( 38 – 41 ). Although evidence exists that alterations in the Treg compartment might contribute to the immunopathology of COVID-19, the literature concerning their functionality and frequency during the acute illness is controversial. Nevertheless, a trend toward functional impairments and decreased levels of circulating Tregs in severe cases of COVID-19 has been reported previously ( 38 – 40 ). It was shown that patients dying from COVID-19 exhibited significantly lower Treg counts and higher Th17/Treg ratio compared to recovered and healthy controls ( 42 – 44 ) and that low Treg counts at hospital admission were associated with clinical worsening and longer duration to discharge ( 45 , 46 ). Correspondingly, several studies demonstrated a downregulation of FoxP3 in severe cases of COVID-19 ( 44 , 47 – 49 ). Given the aforementioned evidence suggesting that an ongoing inflammatory profile, autoantibody formation, inflammatory tissue damage, SARS-CoV-2 persistence and viral reactivation (herpes virus family) likely contribute to the persistence of symptoms, it is conceivable that Tregs are involved in the pathophysiology of Long COVID ( 50 ). Yet, there exist uncertainties concerning the longitudinal dynamics of the Treg population during recovery from COVID-19, and it remains unclear if Treg dysfunction is involved in the immunopathology of Long COVID. Therefore, we aimed to summarize the existing literature on the frequency (e.g., absolute counts, relative frequency) and functionality (e.g., cytokine secretion, ex vivo suppressive capacity) of Tregs in convalescent COVID-19 patients with and without persisting symptoms and to explore indications for their potential involvement in the development of Long COVID.

molecular_mechanism_and_relationship.activity_type_context: COVID-19 (acute, recovery, asymptomatic, severe, fatal), Long COVID pathophysiology, immune system dysregulation, Omicron variant infection/stimulation.
molecular_mechanism_and_relationship.mechanism_description: Tregs are crucial for immune homeostasis, promoting self-tolerance and preventing excessive inflammation through suppression of effector cells, cytokine secretion (IL-10, IL-35, TGF-β), and IL-2 regulation. In acute severe COVID-19, an exaggerated innate immune response, potentially antagonizing Treg generation and FoxP3 induction, can lead to Th17 cell dominance. This phase is also characterized by acute enrichment of hypoxia-induced transcripts, depletion of Treg-vital factors (dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate, retinoic acid), and potential Treg extravasation or apoptosis. During recovery, higher FoxP3, IL-10, and suppressive function in Tregs of recovered patients suggest a role in disease resolution. In asymptomatic infection, an expansion of HLA class II-expressing Tregs may mediate T helper cell suppression. In Long COVID, persistent Treg dysregulation, potentially linked to post-viral autoimmunity, contributes to immunopathology. However, increased Tregs can also lead to immunosuppression, favoring deficient viral clearance, persistent infections, and cyclical symptom flare-ups. Preliminary evidence suggests the Omicron variant peptide might induce a shift from an effector to a regulatory T cell program by increasing FoxP3 expression.

dose_intensity_and_specificity.dose_comparison_summary: Initial COVID-19 severity influences Long COVID symptoms, with hospitalized patients and those with severe acute disease experiencing more residual symptoms (e.g., respiratory) compared to mild/asymptomatic cases (fatigue-dominant). Reinfections increase the risk of post-acute sequelae. Severe acute COVID-19 is consistently linked to decreased circulating Tregs, functional impairments, lower Treg counts (especially in fatal cases or at hospital admission correlating with worsening prognosis), higher Th17/Treg ratios, and FoxP3 downregulation. Conversely, recovery from severe acute COVID-19 is associated with increased systemic Treg frequency and suppressive function, with peripheral Treg populations normalizing within weeks to months depending on initial severity (mild vs. severe). However, comparisons of total Treg frequencies between recovered patients and controls, or among recovered patients with different initial disease severities, show ambiguous, equivocal, and heterogeneous results, often without clear attribution to severity or time. Notably, the pediatric population showed greater Treg differences. Some longitudinal studies report dynamic changes (e.g., decreasing total Tregs, increasing naïve Tregs, decreasing central memory Tregs, and IL-2 over time), while others suggest a return to equilibrium. Severely ill patients with persistently low CD8+ T cell counts six months post-discharge exhibit higher Treg frequencies. Increased Treg frequency is also associated with longer viral shedding and SARS-CoV-2 positivity. Treg adaptations are highly individual, influenced by age, gender, co-morbidities, and immunological status. Studies on tissue-resident Tregs are predominantly biased towards severe/critical cases.
dose_intensity_and_specificity.specificity_finding: The findings primarily focus on regulatory T cell (Treg) dynamics and associated markers (e.g., FoxP3, IL-10, IL-17) in COVID-19 convalescence and Long COVID. Hypoxia-induced transcripts are specifically enriched in acute COVID-19. Treg adaptations are highly individualized, influenced by various patient factors. While total Treg frequencies often show conflicting directions between convalescent patients and controls, specific Treg subsets or functional markers can provide more distinct insights. Treg dysregulation in Long COVID is heterogeneous, with reported increases and decreases. Treg frequency alone may not fully indicate regulatory capacity. Importantly, Treg identification and characterization are complicated by the lack of exclusive markers and non-standardized phenotyping across studies, leading to varied reported proportions. Furthermore, T cell profiles can differ significantly between tissue and blood compartments. Most reviewed studies involved wild-type SARS-CoV-2 in unvaccinated individuals, which limits generalizability to current variants and vaccinated populations.

clinical_implication_and_population.target_population: Convalescent COVID-19 patients (with and without persistent symptoms, various time points), Long COVID patients (with residual symptoms, post-acute sequelae, or latent autoimmunity), acute COVID-19 patients (mild, moderate, severe, critical, hospitalized, non-hospitalized), patients with reinfections, asymptomatic COVID-19 patients, pediatric population (<15 years) recovering from COVID-19, patients with persistent SARS-CoV-2 infection/viral shedding, fatal COVID-19 cases, and seronegative/healthy controls. Predominantly unvaccinated individuals with wild-type SARS-CoV-2 infections.
clinical_implication_and_population.health_implication: Treg dynamics are critical for understanding COVID-19 progression and long-term sequelae. Dysregulated or compromised immunoregulatory mechanisms involving Tregs contribute to immune system perturbations, dysfunctional immune responses, and the development and persistence of Long COVID symptoms (e.g., chronic inflammation, post-viral autoimmunity). Severe acute COVID-19 is associated with negative disease outcomes, clinical worsening, and acute respiratory distress syndrome due to Treg loss or dysfunction. Conversely, higher Treg function (FoxP3, IL-10, suppressive capacity) or restoration of Tregs during recovery from severe COVID-19 suggests a role in disease resolution and less severe outcomes. Expansion of specific Treg populations in asymptomatic infection may contribute to milder disease courses. However, an increase in Tregs can also lead to immunosuppression, favoring deficient viral clearance and persistent infections, leading to cyclical symptom flare-ups and prolonged viral shedding. Decreased or dysfunctional Tregs (e.g., in fatal cases or those with chronic viral infections and autoimmune complications) are linked to adverse prognoses. Persistently low CD8+ T cell counts in severe illness are linked to higher Treg frequency, while lower effector Treg populations and FoxP3 expression in previously hospitalized patients suggest immune dysregulation. For Long COVID, conflicting findings on Treg frequencies and a lack of functional assessment make definitive health implications unclear, but persistent Treg dysregulation is implicated. Emerging variants may also influence Treg responses and immune evasion.
clinical_implication_and_population.risk_classification: Tregs offer a Protective benefit through their restoration during recovery from severe COVID-19, higher function in recovered patients, and expansion in asymptomatic infections, suggesting roles in disease resolution and T helper cell suppression. However, Adverse risk is associated with Treg loss/dysfunction in severe COVID-19 (leading to immunopathology and poor outcomes), persistent Treg dysregulation in Long COVID, and potentially, excessively high Tregs favoring viral persistence and cyclical symptom flare-ups. Lower effector Treg populations/FoxP3 in hospitalized patients and persistently low CD8+ T cell counts also indicate adverse immune regulation. The heterogeneity and conflicting findings regarding Tregs in Long COVID limit its immediate Diagnostic utility for prognosis and stratification, though further research into Treg frequency/function holds promise.

biomarker_reliability_and_future_focus.reliability_assessment: The reliability of current findings on Treg dynamics, particularly in Long COVID, is limited by several factors. There's a scarcity of studies on Long COVID, leading to inconclusive and often contradictory results regarding Treg frequencies, with no firm conclusions on their causal involvement or association with disease severity/onset time. The exact longitudinal dynamics are elusive due to a lack of acute-phase baseline samples. Methodological heterogeneity is a major issue, including varied phenotyping strategies, non-standardized marker sets (e.g., five different sets for total Treg frequencies), and inconsistent sampling stages, which collectively hinder comparability across studies. Treg identification and isolation are inherently difficult due to their dynamic nature and the lack of exclusively expressed markers. Moreover, an increased Treg frequency does not necessarily equate to greater regulatory capacity, and many studies lack in-depth functional assessment of Tregs, especially in Long COVID. Comparisons of total Treg frequencies between recovered patients and controls, or across different initial disease severities, often yield ambiguous, equivocal, or heterogeneous results. The predominance of studies on wild-type SARS-CoV-2 in unvaccinated individuals also limits the representativeness of findings for contemporary clinical contexts with new variants and vaccinated populations.
recommended_alternatives: Adherence to consensualized/standardized basal phenotyping strategies, minimally including CD4, CD25, CD127, and FoxP3 staining.

Investigating Treg adaptations in association with different symptom clusters and blood parameters (e.g., serological status, cytokine levels, autoantibody titers), beyond sole cell frequency quantification.
Assessing/further investigating Treg functionality (e.g., cytokine secretion of IL-10, IL-17, IL-2, TGF-β, and ex vivo suppressive capacity), particularly in Long COVID patients.
More detailed analysis of Treg subsets in different maturation statuses (e.g., naïve, central memory, effector memory, TEMRA) when total Treg proportions are inconclusive.
Investigation of Treg adaptations in relation to specific SARS-CoV-2 variants, vaccination status, and previous infections.
Investigating Treg frequencies and Th17/Treg ratio correlation with specific Long COVID symptom clusters or laboratory parameters.
